analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations bring foreign profits home at a 5.25 percent tax rate if they promise to reinvest them.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 33 cosponsors from both parties, sat in the Senate Finance Committee for 21 months and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a U.S. company with profits sitting in foreign subsidiaries choose to bring that money home for one year while paying a 5.25 percent tax on it instead of the normal corporate rate of up to 35 percent. To qualify, the company's own chief executive and board would have to approve a plan saying the money would be reinvested in the United States — in hiring and training, infrastructure, research, capital spending, or 'financial stabilization' aimed at keeping or creating jobs. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large U.S. multinational corporations with accumulated foreign earnings. They would pay roughly one-seventh of the normal tax rate on profits repatriated under the election, and their own officers — not a government agency — would define and approve the reinvestment plan that unlocks the rate.

how_it_helps.text: A U.S. corporation doing business abroad could elect to pay a 5.25 percent tax on its excess foreign dividends brought home for one year, in place of the regular corporate tax or the alternative minimum tax on those amounts.

To qualify, the repatriated dividends must be described in a domestic reinvestment plan covering worker hiring and training, infrastructure, research and development, capital investment, or financial stabilization of the corporation for job retention or creation.
The reinvestment plan is approved by the taxpayer's own president or chief executive and its board of directors — no government agency signs off on whether the spending actually creates jobs.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Earnings that would otherwise be taxed at the full corporate rate of up to 35 percent would be taxed at 5.25 percent, and the bill would also cut the company's foreign tax credits on those amounts by 85 percent. The foregone revenue is borne by the rest of the taxpaying public.

drawbacks.text: The plan that unlocks the 5.25 percent rate can include 'financial stabilization of the corporation' for job retention or creation, a category broad enough to cover uses such as paying down debt, and it is written and approved by the company's own executives rather than any outside reviewer.

The 5.25 percent rate is a small fraction of the normal up-to-35 percent corporate tax on repatriated earnings, so the direct fiscal effect is a large reduction in tax collected on profits the companies had already earned.

A concern supporters of such holidays generally acknowledge: because corporate cash is fungible, a company can bring home money it would have repatriated anyway and redirect its planned domestic spending into the reinvestment plan, so the promised job gains may largely relabel spending rather than add to it. The bill's own structure — self-drafted plans with no job-creation verification — offers no mechanism to prevent that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose is job creation, but its only firm benefit is a steep tax cut for multinationals with offshore earnings; the job gains depend entirely on spending categories the companies define for themselves, with no verification. The certain cost is foregone federal revenue at a time of rising deficits. As drafted, the guaranteed winners are the electing corporations, and the public benefit is speculative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. John Ensign introduced the bill on March 11, 2003, with five original cosponsors including Democrats Barbara Boxer and Evan Bayh.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that committee referral was the only formal step the bill ever took.
Thirty-three senators signed on as cosponsors — 24 Republicans and 9 Democrats.

The only later entries in the action history are a star print order in March 2003 and repeated introductory remarks by the sponsor in March 2004; there were no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still in committee, so it died without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations with offshore earnings came out ahead: they faced no pressure to repatriate profits under this bill's terms and continued operating under the existing system of deferring U.S. tax on foreign profits. The Treasury avoided the revenue loss the bill would have caused, but the public got neither the promised job-creation investment nor any tax on the offshore earnings. A version of this repatriation-holiday idea was later enacted in 2004 as one piece of a much larger corporate tax bill, not through this bill.

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it in floor remarks at introduction in March 2003 and again in March 2004.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Barbara Boxer (original cosponsor) and Evan Bayh
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the day of introduction.

against.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained in committee from referral in March 2003 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 33 cosponsors split 24 Republicans and 9 Democrats, with two Democrats among the original cosponsors — and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan division on the merits.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with foreign earnings
industries.note: The bill would have cut their tax to 5.25 percent on profits brought home, versus the normal up-to-35 percent rate, with reinvestment plans self-drafted and self-approved by company executives. The industry's gain is federal revenue the public would otherwise collect; the promised jobs and investment are unverified because the bill contains no enforcement mechanism.

Companies with no foreign subsidiaries could not use the 5.25 percent rate, so the bill would have deepened the tax advantage of multinationals over domestic competitors. Ordinary consumers see little direct effect either way.
